newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia seen flexing muscles in mining sector.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia seen flexing muscles in mining sector.

text.p: Indonesia's proposed changes to mining rules are an attempt to recover some face after the humiliating Busang scandal, analysts and industry sources said on Thursday.
"The government is still suffering from the Busang syndrome," said Hartojo Wignjowijoto, senior economist with the private Asian Pacific Economic Consultancy Indonesia.
"It is trying to show the people that it is still sovereign in Indonesia and has control over the country's natural resources," he told Reuters. "It's a political year."

The government and some well-connected local companies clamoured for a slice of the Busang cake, but were embarrassed when an independent audit found that the property was almost worthless -- instead of being the century's biggest gold find.
Canadian mining company Bre-X Minerals Ltd had declared that Busang contained 71 million ounces of gold.

The scandal led to the sacking of the director-general of mining and the mines and energy ministry's secretary-general, and sparked calls for increased government control over the rapidly expanding foreign-dominated mining sector.

Foreign mining companies were informed earlier this week of the proposed changes to the seventh-generation contract of work (COW), which included requiring them to allocate a 10 percent stake to the government for free in future ventures.
The government stake is to be increased when additional reserves are discovered and/or if annual production is above the level approved by the government during the feasibility study.

The government was also seeking a share of capital gains made by a mining company operating in Indonesia or its holding entity when their share prices rise due to information announced by the company operating in the country.

The proposals also require estimates of reserves to be made by an independent consultant, and that by the sixth year of operations, all posts other than those of directors must be filled by Indonesians.

"I think the government is using the proposals as leverage," economist Hartojo said. "I think there will be give and take. It may soften the terms. The government will not want to kill the goose that lays golden eggs."
Analysts said there appeared to have been a lack of consultation within the government itself over the proposals.
State Secretary Murdiono said the government would be consistent in applying mining rules which currently allow 100 percent foreign-owned companies to operate.
Investment Minister Sanyoto Sastrowardoyo was more blunt. "It is a new thing. I don't know what the reasons are or the motivation," he said.

Senior international mining sources said the proposed COW changes could jeopardise the whole investment climate in Indonesia, whose economic growth has been fuelled to a large part by foreign direct investment.

"The changes will give rise to a whole new rethink on Indonesia as an area to invest in," one source said. "Mining firms would have to go back to their boards for agreement on the changes, but they have virtually no time to do this."
M. Simatupang, vice-chairman of the Indonesian Mining Association, said foreign mining companies have been given until Tuesday by the government to respond to the proposed changes.
"We are very concerned that this (may) damage the investment climate, which the government is promoting," he said. "There are about 60 companies which have applied for about 170 COW."
A foreign mining executive said the proposals were linked to nationalistic interests. "It has been coming the last six months and surfaced with the Busang incident.

"If the terms and conditions are not satisfactory, and the mine is not economic with the carried interests, then it (project) doesn't proceed," he said. "What we will see is a downturn in the mining industry, particularly with new mines."
